statement.informal: The classical Poisson disk/square sandwich D(R) ≤ S(R) ≤ D(R√2), where D(R) is the Cartesian iterated quarter-disk integral ∫₀ᴿ exp(-x²)·gaussianI(√(R²-x²)) dx and S(R) := gaussianI(R)². This is the FIRST HALF of the standard two-dimensional proof that ∫₀^∞ exp(-t²)dt = √π/2 (squeeze D(R) and D(R√2) between the SAME S(R) as R→∞, using polar coordinates to evaluate D directly). Proven completely and correctly in MachLib's Mathlib-free base (disk_le_square, square_le_disk_sqrt2, GaussianDiskSandwich.lean) -- but STRANDED as a route to √π: closing the classical argument needs D(R)'s OWN derivative in R, which requires genuine two-dimensional polar-coordinate integration (the Jacobian r dr dθ transforming BOTH integration variables at once). MachLib's real-analysis base is one-dimensional only and has no such machinery. The theorem stands as a correct, complete, standalone result; the project's actual finish line (gaussianImproperIntegral_eq_sqrt_pi_div_two) instead used a Laplace/Feynman parameter-differentiation trick that never leaves one dimension.

common_mistakes.tactic: attempting to finish sqrt(pi) via D(R)'s own derivative in R (angle substitution x=Rsin(theta))
common_mistakes.why_fails: The substitution itself is clean (existing FTC/chain-rule machinery), but d/dR of the resulting integrand leaves a residual term with gaussianI(Rcos(theta)) still present, non-elementary, not telescoping to anything recognizable -- the real classical argument needs genuine 2D polar coordinates (transforming BOTH integration variables via the Jacobian r dr dtheta), which a 1D-only real-analysis base does not have. A partial 1D substitution on just the outer variable is not a substitute for that. Confirmed via paper analysis BEFORE attempting the Lean proof -- do not re-attempt without first building genuine multivariable/polar integration.

common_mistakes.tactic: treating this as wasted work once the pivot happened
common_mistakes.why_fails: It is not -- disk_le_square and square_le_disk_sqrt2 are both complete, sorryAx-free, zero-new-axiom theorems in their own right, useful for anyone who DOES build 2D polar integration later. Abandoning a route because its OWN extension is hard is different from the route being wrong; the sandwich itself is correct.
